title: How Teachers Can Protect Their Energy in a System That Treats Them Like Children
author: Debbie Thompson
summary: Debbie Thompson, who has taught for 24 years in large English secondary schools, describes how senior leaders can fall into treating teachers as students, demanding compliance and punishing disagreement. She recounts a case in which a senior colleague blamed her for a class that was deliberately disrupting her lessons and, after a confrontation, the head teacher told her she was not a good fit. Thompson argues that Ofsted pressure drives fear-based leadership, that compliance is mistaken for professionalism, and that schools promote leaders for data skills over emotional maturity. She then offers practical strategies: treat observation feedback as one person's opinion, use calm boundary phrases, keep a daily written record, find a supportive colleague, and remember that a leader's behaviour reflects on them. She also advises protecting energy outside school and, when all else fails, leaving a damaging school.
points: Thompson ties infantilising leadership to Ofsted pressure, arguing that leaders who feel watched shift into fear-driven control and treat staff as risks rather than colleagues.
She argues schools mistake compliance for professionalism, so disagreement is read as disloyalty and can lead to teachers being managed out.
Non-confrontational boundary phrases such as asking for feedback in writing give teachers a concrete way to protect their energy.
Keeping a short daily written record guards against being gaslit about one's competence.
Her closing advice is that leaving a school that is making you ill can be the healthiest choice, once talking strategies have been tried.
quotes: When leaders aren’t emotionally aware, they unconsciously repeat the teacher–student dynamic with staff.
I believe that OFSTED is one of the biggest drivers of unhealthy school culture.

This control mode is driven by fear and it can lead to them micromanaging good teachers, clamping down on dissent, punishing disagreement and lead to them treating staff as risks rather than colleagues.
In many English schools, there’s an unspoken belief that good teachers don’t push back, professionalism equals obedience, and disagreement equals negativity.
I’ve noticed that weak leaders use power to silence people, whereas strong leaders use power to support people.
So a school can end up with leaders who are technically competent but emotionally underdeveloped. And emotionally underdeveloped leaders often treat adults like children.
That record helped to ground me and protect me. It helped prevent me from being gaslit by senior staff who could try to persuade me that I was not a good teacher.
Until the system changes, protect your energy fiercely. Your well-being is not optional, and your dignity is not negotiable.
